quoted_clause: 6.24M requests/month × 9,500 tokens ≈ 5.93×10¹⁰ tokens/month
observed: The 6.24M requests/month figure is referenced from Ch 16 §16.3 but is not derivable from the canonical 10 rps average stated in this chapter. 10 rps × 86,400 s/day × 30 days = 25.92M requests/month, which is 4.15× the 6.24M. The 6.24M implies either a different average rate, a different month length, a duty-cycle factor, or a different traffic model established in Ch 4 or Ch 16.
evidence: 10 × 86,400 × 30 = 25,920,000. 6,240,000 / 10 = 624,000 s = 7.22 days. Neither 7.22 days nor a 24% duty cycle is stated in this chunk. The text says the figure comes from 'Ch16 §16.3' but does not show the derivation.
root_cause: Cross-chapter dependency: the 6.24M is a canonical value from an earlier chapter with a traffic model (possibly business-hours-only, or a different average rate) not restated here.
correction: Add a brief parenthetical showing the derivation or the traffic model that produces 6.24M, e.g., '(Ch 16: 10 rps average over 7.22 effective days/month, reflecting the canonical business-hours traffic model of Ch 4, Table 4-2)' or simply state the effective seconds-per-month used. If the 6.24M comes from a different average rate than 10 rps, clarify which rate is used for the monthly volume calculation.

page_hint: Ch 18, §18.3.1, hardware capacity mapping table, '70B dense 8-bit' row
quoted_clause: 1 (weights alone fit on 1×H100, leaving 7 GPUs; with the canonical KV budget the 8×H100 pool still holds weights + KV)
observed: The '1×H100' in the parenthetical could be misread as the deployment configuration (i.e., the model runs on one GPU with the other seven idle). In reality, the model would be TP across all 8 GPUs (or at least use more than 1 GPU) to get sufficient KV space for the canonical 9.5K-token request. On a single 80 GB H100, only 10 GB remains for KV (80 − 70), which holds ~3,800 tokens at 2.62 MB/token — far short of the 9,500 needed. The parenthetical's second clause ('the 8×H100 pool still holds weights + KV') corrects this, but the initial '1×H100' creates a moment of confusion.
evidence: 80 GB − 70 GB = 10 GB KV on 1 GPU. 10 GB / 2.62 MB/token ≈ 3,817 tokens < 9,500. The model cannot serve the canonical request on 1 GPU. The '1×H100' is a minimum-hardware statement, not a deployment statement, but the table's column header is '# fit on 8×H100' which makes the '1' look like a deployment count.
root_cause: The table conflates 'minimum hardware for weights' with 'deployment configuration.' The parenthetical tries to disambiguate but the initial '1×H100' is the first thing the reader sees.
correction: Reword the parenthetical to make the minimum-vs-deployment distinction explicit: '1 (minimum: 70 GB weights fit on a single 80 GB H100; deployment: TP across the full 8×H100 pool so the 570 GB residual holds the canonical KV budget).' Alternatively, add a footnote to the table: 'The # fit column counts model instances that can co-reside on the 8×H100 pool; the parenthetical notes the minimum hardware for weights only — the actual deployment uses the full pool for KV.'
acceptance_test: A reader who stops at '1×H100' does not conclude the 8-bit model is deployed on a single GPU; the text makes clear that the deployment uses the full 8×H100 pool for KV.

quoted_clause: The 120/250/300/800 ms values are illustrative per-request latencies for a short-prompt routing scenario (the kind of request a router triages in milliseconds)
observed: The scope note correctly distinguishes the routing-scenario latencies from the canonical 8.6 s service time. However, the phrase 'the kind of request a router triages in milliseconds' is slightly misleading: the router does not 'triage in milliseconds' — the router makes a routing decision in microseconds, and the 120–800 ms is the model's service time for a short prompt, not the router's decision time. The reader might conflate the router's decision latency with the model's service latency.
evidence: The 120/250/300/800 ms values are in the 'Per-request service latency (ms)' column of Table 18-2, which is the model's end-to-end service time for a short prompt. The router's own decision time (feature extraction, cost lookup, dispatch) is on the order of microseconds to low milliseconds and is not what the table measures.
root_cause: The parenthetical 'the kind of request a router triages in milliseconds' uses 'triage' in a way that could be read as describing the router's processing time rather than the request's service time.
correction: Reword to: 'illustrative per-request model service latencies for a short-prompt routing scenario (sub-second requests that a router dispatches to the appropriate model tier; the router's own decision time is negligible relative to these values).' This separates the router's decision time from the model's service time.
acceptance_test: A reader does not conclude that the 120–800 ms values include the router's processing time; the model service time and the router decision time are clearly separated.

quoted_clause: Consolidate when: workload profile overlap ≥70%, latency tolerance ≥300 ms, and cost differential >30%
observed: The three thresholds (≥70%, ≥300 ms, >30%) are stated as design criteria without an evidence label. They are reasonable engineering heuristics but are presented with the same authority as the derived arithmetic. The text does note 'our scenario sits exactly at the threshold' which is honest, but the thresholds themselves should be marked as illustrative design criteria, not universal rules.
evidence: No [ILLUSTRATIVE] or [ASSUMPTION] label on the three thresholds. The '≥70%' overlap, '≥300 ms' latency tolerance, and '>30%' cost differential are specific numbers that a reader might adopt as universal criteria.
root_cause: The thresholds are design heuristics for the worked example, not derived from a formal analysis or a universal standard.
correction: Add: 'These thresholds are [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] design criteria for the worked example; a deployment should set its own consolidation thresholds based on its specific SLO, cost model, and workload mix.'
acceptance_test: The three thresholds carry an evidence label and are scoped to the worked example rather than presented as universal rules.

quoted_clause: 1 (weights alone fit on 1×H100, leaving 7 GPUs; with the canonical KV budget the 8×H100 pool still holds weights + KV)
observed: The parenthetical states two seemingly contradictory facts: the 8-bit model fits on 1 GPU (leaving 7 free) and the 8×H100 pool holds weights + KV. These refer to different models (8-bit vs FP16) but the parenthetical does not clarify this attribution.
evidence: The 8-bit model (70 GB) fits on 1 H100 (80 GB), leaving 7 GPUs free. The FP16 model (140 GB) uses the full 8-GPU pool for weights + KV. The parenthetical conflates these two facts about different models in one cell.
root_cause: Parenthetical tries to state facts about two different models simultaneously without attributing each claim.
correction: Clarify that 'leaving 7 GPUs' refers to the 8-bit model's weight placement, while 'the 8×H100 pool still holds weights + KV' refers to the canonical FP16 deployment. Or remove the second clause if it is not essential to this table cell.
acceptance_test: The parenthetical unambiguously attributes each claim to the correct model.

quoted_clause: the input tokens billed across the task's calls are amplified by the agentic factor *α* from Section 4 (cumulative-context total vs the single-shot equivalent)
observed: §6 states that billed input tokens are amplified by α, but §4 explicitly states α is NOT the billed token multiplier: "It is not the total model-processed or API-billed token multiplier." Under the no-prefix-cache policy, billed input amplification at T=3 is 41,990/9,200 ≈ 4.56×, not α ≈ 1.27×. Under perfect prefix cache it is 11,795/9,200 ≈ 1.28× ≈ α. The §6 claim is only true under perfect prefix caching, and the cache policy is not specified.
evidence: §4: "α measures retained/accumulated task context... It is not the total model-processed or API-billed token multiplier." §4 event ledger: task_input = 41,990 at T=3 (no-reuse), billed no-cache = 42,485 total. 42,485/9,500 ≈ 4.47× vs α(3) = 1.27×. Under perfect cache: 12,290/9,500 ≈ 1.29× ≈ α. The §6 comment tells the reader to use α as the billed amplifier without stating the cache policy.
root_cause: §6 cost formula comment conflates retained-context amplification (α) with billed-token amplification, contradicting §4's explicit warning.
correction: Either (a) specify "under perfect prefix caching, billed input is approximately α × single-shot input" and note that under no caching the amplification is ~4.5×, or (b) replace α with the correct billed-token multiplier for the stated policy, or (c) remove the claim that α amplifies billed tokens and instead say the cost formula's tokens/call term must be computed from the execution-trace totals under the stated cache policy.
acceptance_test: After correction, §6's cost formula comment must not state or imply that α is the billed-token multiplier without specifying a cache policy under which that is true, and must not contradict §4's explicit statement that α is not the billed multiplier.

page_hint: Ch 19 §4 'Tool-call latency budget' (printed page not verified — chunk supplied without pagination); propagates to Table 19-1, §7, §8
quoted_clause: On 8×H100 the per-turn agent step averages ~120 ms for a 10,000-token context; tool backends (search, SQL) add 50–150 ms depending on data volume. So per-turn orchestration overhead *L*agent ≈ 220 ms (median).
observed: The 120 ms per-turn 'agent step' is inconsistent with the chapter's own per-turn model cost by roughly an order of magnitude, and the inconsistency is invisible because the two quantities are both labelled 'per turn'.
evidence: Under the chapter's own per-turn convention each turn is one model invocation that emits γ=65 reasoning tokens and a tool call. Prefill of a 10,000-token context at the canonical 1.08 s / 9,200 tokens = 1.174 s; decode of 65 tokens at 25 ms/token = 1.625 s; so one per-turn model invocation ≈ 2.80 s. Even under a perfect prefix cache the decode of 65 reasoning tokens alone is 1.63 s — 13x the quoted 120 ms. The chapter's own W model agrees: W(3)-W(2) = 17.704-14.561 = 3.14 s and W(2)-W(1) = 14.561-11.520 = 3.04 s of marginal cost per additional turn, versus the 220 ms quoted. The 220 ms figure therefore cannot be 'the LLM's short decision step'; it can only be non-model orchestration overhead.
root_cause: λ_step was introduced as a 'decision step' cost without being reconciled against the per-turn model invocation cost that W already carries. Two different quantities share the name 'per-turn overhead', and the reader is invited to budget 220 ms/turn for a step that the chapter's own arithmetic prices at ~3 s.
correction: Rename λ_step to 'orchestration overhead excluding model compute' and state in the same sentence that the model's own per-turn cost (prefill of the grown prefix + decode of γ) is carried inside W. If a genuine model-step latency is wanted, derive it (e.g. ~1.17 s prefill + 1.63 s decode under no-reuse) and use it consistently. Add a one-line reconciliation table: per-turn cost = model prefill + model decode + tool round-trip + orchestration.
acceptance_test: Every per-turn latency number in Ch 19 (Table 19-1 rows, §4, §7, §8, mini-case) either (a) explicitly excludes model compute and says so, or (b) equals the marginal per-turn cost implied by W (≈3.0-3.1 s). No two per-turn figures may differ by more than the stated scope difference, and the '<1 s orchestration SLA' scoping in §8 must name which quantity it bounds.

page_hint: Ch 19 §4, Tool-call latency budget and W(T) scope note
quoted_clause: λ_tool ≈ 100 ms (median, tool backend) ... The tool/retrieval leg here uses Chapter 17's ~133 ms/turn rate
observed: Two different tool-backend rates are used for the same conceptual quantity: λ_tool ≈ 100 ms in L_agent (the orchestration overhead) and λ_tool/retr ≈ 133 ms in W (the full service time). The text acknowledges the inconsistency ("Chapter 17 §8 itself notes that a single model should use one rate consistently") but does not resolve it. page_hint: Ch 19 §8 'Unconditional fallback-inclusive ledger' paragraph; contradicted by Ch 19 §7
quoted_clause: Under the fallback-inclusive ledger the unconditional p95 equals the conditional p95 — the fallback occupies only the top 2% — mass entirely above p95 — so it cannot move the 95th percentile (under the zero-turn convention it lands exactly on the boundary, CDF(*T* ≤ 2) = 95.0%, and reads *T* = 2 → 440 ms — which is exactly why the convention must travel with the number)
observed: One sentence asserts two different values for the same percentile, and the CDF quoted inside the parenthetical is false under the convention the sentence is about.
evidence: Ledger distribution (added orchestration): 68% @ 220 ms, 25% @ 440 ms, 5% @ 660 ms, 2% @ 860 ms. CDF(440) = 93.0%, CDF(660) = 98.0% → unconditional p95 = 660 ms, p99 = 860 ms (which is what §7 states). Under the zero-turn convention (fallback at 0 ms) CDF(440) = 2+68+25 = 95.0% → p95 = 440 ms, p99 = 660 ms. The parenthetical's '95.0%' belongs to the zero-turn convention, not to the fallback-inclusive ledger the sentence is describing; and under the zero-turn convention the fallback sits at the bottom of the distribution, not 'on the boundary' of the top.
root_cause: Two percentile conventions are interleaved in one sentence without labels, and the parenthetical's arithmetic was computed under the other convention.
correction: Split into two labelled statements: (a) fallback-inclusive ledger: CDF(T<=2) = 93.0%, CDF(T<=3) = 98.0% → p95 = 660 ms, p99 = 860 ms; (b) zero-turn convention: CDF(T<=2) = 95.0% → p95 = 440 ms, p99 = 660 ms. Keep §7's cross-reference consistent with (a).
acceptance_test: Each percentile is stated once per convention together with its CDF; no sentence contains two values for the same percentile; §7's 'same p95 but p99 = 860 ms' matches the labelled ledger statement.

quoted_clause: λ_step ≈ 120 ms (the model's tool-call decision step)
observed: The 120 ms is labelled 'the model's tool-call decision step' and is part of L_agent (the 'loop around the model'). However, W(T) already includes the model's prefill and decode for every invocation (Σ T_prefill + 25 ms/token × all generated tokens). If the 120 ms is model computation, it is double-counted relative to W. If it is system/scheduling overhead (queueing, context setup, kernel launch), calling it 'the model's' is misleading.
evidence: W(3) = 4.93 s prefill + 12.375 s decode + 0.399 s tool. The prefill and decode terms already account for the model reading the context and generating γ + tool-call tokens. The text explicitly states 'W already carries the per-turn model work inside the γ decode.' The 120 ms in L_agent is a separate, smaller quantity, but its physical meaning is not stated.
root_cause: The 120 ms likely represents per-invocation system overhead (scheduling, KV-cache setup, kernel launch latency) that is not captured by the idealised prefill+decode arithmetic in W, but the label 'the model's tool-call decision step' reads as model computation.
correction: Rename or re-describe λ_step. For example: 'λ_step ≈ 120 ms (per-invocation system overhead: scheduling, KV-cache slot allocation, kernel launch — not the model's FLOP time, which is in W's prefill/decode terms).' Alternatively, if it genuinely is a short model generation separate from γ, state that explicitly and show how it is not already in W's decode term.
acceptance_test: A reader can state unambiguously what physical process the 120 ms represents and confirm it is not already included in W's prefill or decode terms.

page_hint: Ch 19 §4, Tool-call latency budget and W(T) scope note
quoted_clause: the LLM's short decision step to formulate the tool call ... averages ~120 ms for a 10,000-token context
observed: The 120 ms "model's tool-call decision step" in L_agent is not clearly related to the γ decode in W. In the per-turn convention, each turn is one model invocation producing γ = 65 tokens, which at 25 ms/token takes 1,625 ms. The 120 ms corresponds to ~4.8 tokens at 25 ms/token. The text does not explain whether the 120 ms is (a) a subset of the 65-token output (the tool-call portion) or (b) a separate short generation. If (a), the remaining ~60 tokens (1,500 ms) of reasoning are not counted in L_agent; if (b), the per-turn convention (one invocation) is inconsistent.
evidence: 120 ms / 25 ms per token = 4.8 tokens. γ = 65 tokens × 25 ms = 1,625 ms. The text says L_agent includes "the LLM's short decision step" (120 ms) but W includes the full γ decode (1,625 ms). The relationship between these two quantities is not stated.
root_cause: L_agent and W decompose the model's per-turn work differently without an explicit mapping.
correction: State explicitly: "The 120 ms is the decode time for the ~5 tool-call tokens within the 65-token γ output; the remaining ~60 reasoning tokens (~1,500 ms) are counted in W's γ decode, not in L_agent." Or, if the 120 ms is a separate generation, reconcile it with the one-invocation-per-turn convention.
acceptance_test: A reader can determine which portion of the model's per-turn time is counted in L_agent and which is counted in W, and the two decompositions are consistent with the one-invocation-per-turn convention.

quoted_clause: **Boundary rule.** A call's *input* never contains output tokens, so `task_input` must sum per-call inputs only — never the “Total tokens (incl. 300 output)” column
observed: The rule as written is false against the chapter's own ledger: a later call's input does contain earlier calls' output tokens.
evidence: Ledger row 2 has input 10,065 = 9,200 + call 1's 65 output tokens + call 1's 800 tool-output tokens. Row 3's input 10,930 likewise contains calls 1-2's outputs. The rule is only true of a call's *own* output.
root_cause: The rule was written to stop the reader adding the 300 final-output tokens to an input sum, but was phrased as a universal property of inputs, which contradicts the ledger printed immediately above it.
correction: Rewrite as: 'A call's own output is never part of its own input; a later call's input does contain earlier calls' outputs and tool results — which is exactly why Σ per-call inputs double-counts carried context and why Σ per-call inputs (41,990) exceeds the retained context (12,095).'
acceptance_test: The boundary rule is true of every row of the ledger printed above it; a reader can apply it without contradiction.

page_hint: §4, 'Multi-step reasoning cost', W formula tool leg; Table 19-1 'Tool latency (median)' row
quoted_clause: The tool/retrieval leg here uses Chapter 17's ~133 ms/turn rate; the chapter's own T·L_agent (~220 ms/turn) is the orchestration-only incremental overhead, a different quantity

The text acknowledges they are 'a different quantity' and quotes Ch 17's note that 'a single model should use one rate consistently,' but never explains why the numbers differ or which components each includes.

quoted_clause: model calls/task × tokens/call × $/token
observed: The cost formula uses "tokens/call" as if it were a single value, but tokens per call varies across calls in the event-level ledger (9,200 for call 1, 10,065 for call 2, 10,930 for call 3, 11,795 for call 4 at T=3). The ≈ sign indicates approximation, but the simplification is not acknowledged.
evidence: Event ledger: call inputs are 9,200 / 10,065 / 10,930 / 11,795. A single "tokens/call" cannot represent these.

correction: Either note that "tokens/call" is an average across calls and varies with T, or rewrite as Σ over calls of input(call_i) × $/input-token + Σ over calls of output(call_i) × $/output-token.

page_hint: Ch 19 §4 'Multi-step reasoning cost' (W(T) definition and the no-reuse / reuse lead calculations); Table 19-1 W rows
quoted_clause: yields a prefill sum of (41,990 / 9,200) × 1.08 ≈ 4.93 s
observed: The W evaluator scales prefill time linearly in token count, contradicting the book's own attention accounting (Ch 22 Table 22-1), so W understates the prefill leg and the error grows with turn count.
evidence: Case-(ii) prefill FLOPs at the four call lengths 9,200 / 10,065 / 10,930 / 11,795 are 1.5099 / 1.6747 / 1.8434 / 2.0160 PFLOP (sum 7.044) versus the linear-only sum 1.288 + 1.4091 + 1.5302 + 1.6513 = 5.879 — a ratio of 1.198. Case (iii) gives ≈1.10. So W_no-reuse(3) ≈ 18.2-18.7 s rather than 17.70 s, and the gap widens with T (the T=4 case is worse still). The chapter elsewhere insists the quadratic term is ~17% of prefill FLOPs at 9.2K and grows with context.
root_cause: The evaluator inherits a linear prefill model from the single-request case and does not carry the quadratic attention term the book derives two chapters later; the W numbers are then used for fleet sizing in Ch 17.
correction: State the prefill-scaling assumption inside the W definition ('prefill time proportional to tokens, case (i) linear-only') and add a sensitivity line giving W(3) under case (ii) and case (iii); or compute the prefill sum from the case-(ii) FLOPs.
acceptance_test: The W definition names its prefill-scaling assumption; the chapter states W(3) under at least one attention-aware case; and Ch 17's fleet sizing cites which W variant it used.

quoted_clause: At the canonical workload's ~86 average in-flight requests at 10 rps (L_exec = λ × W_exec ≈ 10 × 8.6 per Ch 4; distinct from the ~100 active-user population) with the median single-turn profile (~27.2 GB/request at 10,365 tokens), the aggregate KV alone is ~86 × 27.2 GB ≈ 2.3 TB
observed: The in-flight count (86) is computed from the single-shot service time (8.6 s), but the per-request KV (27.2 GB) is from the T=1 agentic profile. If the agentic service time (W(1) ≈ 11.52 s no-reuse) were used, in-flight would be ~115 and aggregate KV ~3.1 TB. The 2.3 TB figure is therefore a lower bound, but the text does not say so.
evidence: Little's Law: L = λW. With W = 8.6 s (single-shot), L = 86. With W = 11.52 s (T=1 agentic, no-reuse), L = 115.2. The text mixes the two: 86 (from single-shot W) × 27.2 GB (from agentic T=1).
root_cause: The 86 figure is imported from Ch 4's base-system calculation. The text uses it for the agentic KV argument without noting that the agentic service time would increase the in-flight count.
correction: Add a brief qualifier: 'Using the base-system in-flight count (86, from Ch 4's 8.6 s service time) as a lower bound — the agentic T=1 service time of ~11.5 s would raise this to ~115 — the aggregate KV is already ~2.3 TB, far beyond one host's 436 GB budget.' This preserves the argument's force while being honest about the conservative estimate.
acceptance_test: The text explicitly states whether the 86 in-flight figure is a lower bound, exact, or upper bound for the agentic case, and the reader can see that the conclusion (KV >> 436 GB) is robust to the choice.
